study_identification.title: Judged by your neighbors: A novel framework for personalized assessment of brain structural aging effects in diverse populations

study_characteristics.study_objective: To introduce and validate a new framework, Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N3), for personalized assessment of brain structural aging. The study aims to show that N3 can better distinguish pathological alterations from natural inter-individual variability compared to traditional normative modeling and brain age models.

dataset_name.reason: The paper clearly lists the datasets used for training, testing, and stability analysis.
dataset_name.supporting_text: Neuroimaging data from six different studies were provided by the respective consortia. Our study includes data from the German National Cohort (NAKO)[61-63], the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) [64], the Münster-Marburg Affective Disorder Cohort (MACS) [65], the Australian Imaging, Biomarker Lifestyle Study of Aging (AIBL) [66], the Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration Neuroimaging Initiative (NIFD), and the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies 3 (OASIS3) [67, 68].

hc_n.reason: The paper states the number of participants in the normative reference sample (NAKO cohort) after exclusions.
hc_n.supporting_text: The training data for fitting models of the different normative modeling approaches comprised 30,047 samples from the population-based NAKO cohort (for details see below). We exclude age groups below 22 years and above 72 years due to small sample sizes (n < 100), which restricts the final sample to 29,883.

imaging_modality.supporting_text: All neuroimaging data utilized in this study were T1-weighted MRI scans from these baseline measurements.

analysis_level.supporting_text: Our analysis focuses on gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), hyperintense white matter (WMH), total intracranial volume (TIV) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volumes.

site_effect_handling.supporting_text: The model was adjusted for potential confounders, including age, age squared (to mitigate non-linear effects), sex and scanner.

site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper provides details on how site effects were handled, both in the statistical analysis and through the N3 methodology.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: The model was adjusted for potential confounders, including age, age squared (to mitigate non-linear effects), sex and scanner. In our application to brain structure, we stratify the training sample by sex and age, resulting into 100 control groups containing same-aged females or males (22 to 72 years), respectively.

model_origin.reason: The paper introduces the N3 framework as a novel approach.
model_origin.supporting_text: We introduce Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N3), a novel framework designed to resolve the confound between natural diversity and subtle pathological patterns.

model_origin_detail.reason: The model is new, not pre-trained.

modeling_method.reason: The paper clearly describes the modeling method as Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N3), which is based on local density estimation.
modeling_method.supporting_text: The N3 approach is based on local density estimation in tailored control groups. To establish a normative reference for the local density seen in a representative sample, we here use the simple and intuitive Nearest-Neighbor algorithm [25, 32].

software_tool.supporting_text: Code to realize the normativity estimation calculations within the N3 framework is written in the Python programming language and is provided as an open-source resource to the scientific community on Github (link tbd).

response_variable.supporting_text: Our analysis focuses on gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), hyperintense white matter (WMH), total intracranial volume (TIV) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volumes.

predictor_variables.supporting_text: In our application to brain structure, we stratify the training sample by sex and age, resulting into 100 control groups containing same-aged females or males (22 to 72 years), respectively.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Validation subsets included n=835 healthy control participants from the MACS study which predominantly comprises younger and middle-aged adults, and an additional n=1073 healthy older adults from the ADNI study to span a wider age demographic

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Applying the normative models to evaluate brain structure of both cognitively healthy and diseased individuals, we validate the ability of each biomarker to differentiate between healthy inter-individual variability and (early) states of pathological decline.

deviation_metric.supporting_text: The final N3 marker indicates how common a brain structural normativity profile is in the chronological age group of the individual.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: The study used ANOVA to assess the explanatory power of the normativity markers, with adjustments for confounders like age, sex, and scanner. Machine learning models (SVM) were used to evaluate predictive performance with metrics like balanced accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: The N3 framework provides a more effective biomarker for detecting neurodegenerative diseases by better accounting for inter-individual variability compared to existing methods.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The N3 marker showed superior performance in distinguishing individuals with Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD), and Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) from healthy controls. It demonstrated larger effect sizes in statistical tests (e.g., η2=0.29 for AD, η2=0.38 for FTD) and higher accuracy in machine learning predictions (e.g., 5.8% improvement for AD, 7.5% for FTD in balanced accuracy) compared to traditional normative models and the Brain Age Gap.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The main limitations are the requirement for large sample sizes, the dependency on the choice of the density estimation algorithm, and the selection of the k parameter for the Nearest Neighbor algorithm.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The N3 framework is presented as a versatile tool applicable to various medical domains beyond brain structure, aiming to advance personalized medicine by providing a more nuanced understanding of individual variability.

general_notes.general_notes: This paper introduces a novel normative modeling framework called Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N3). The method is designed to better account for inter-individual variability in brain structure and aging. The authors demonstrate its superiority over traditional normative modeling and brain age models in detecting neurodegenerative diseases (MCI, AD, FTD) using a large neuroimaging dataset. The code for the N3 framework is intended to be released as an open-source tool.
